title: How to detect ban evasion
summary: How to detect ban evasion: compare a new account with a banned one on handle, email, phone, photos and timing. Sixtyfour traces where each identifier leads.
body_markdown:
Ban evasion is getting round a suspension or ban to come back to a platform, for example by opening a new account under a different name or by reusing an account that already exists. The Trust & Safety Professional Association calls it recidivism, and each platform sets its edges in its own rules: Discord's covers new accounts and reused existing ones, and YouTube's covers channels a terminated creator creates, acquires or is repeatedly or prominently featured in. On Reddit, ban evasion drew more permanent bans from the admins than any other rule in the second half of 2025: 1,446,274 of them.


Compare it with the banned account on handle and email patterns, the phone number's block and line type, reused photos and text, and how soon after the ban it appeared, then check whether both accounts lead to the same person in public records. Weigh each link by how unusual the shared value is and whether it is independent of the others. Treat the account as the banned user only when at least two strong, independent links agree, and record what stays open.


Often within days, though not always. In a study of 8,551 pairs of banned Wikipedia accounts and the evasion accounts that followed them, the new account was created a median of about four days and 20 hours after the ban, with a standard deviation of 255 days. A new account soon after a ban fits evasion, and a long gap does not rule it out.


Not on its own. A similar username counts for more when it is unusual and the new account appeared soon after the ban, and for little when it is built from a common word, a first name or a year. Research on Wikipedia found that many evaders come back with a similar name and that the evasion accounts which outlasted the accounts they replaced had less similar ones, so a different name does not clear an account either.


Treat a shared surname, town or household as context, never as a link. Check whether the new account has its own history, such as its own email address, photos and public footprint from before the ban, and act only if it shares specific traces with the banned account that a relative would not. Wikipedia's sockpuppetry policy warns that when family members, roommates or co-workers share a computer, their accounts "risk being accused of sockpuppetry".


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes a new account's handle, email address or phone number, researches where each appears across public sources and whether they lead to the person behind the banned account, and returns every link with its source and, when you ask for one, a confidence score. Anything it could not establish is reported as open, and a person on your team decides.


No. Researchers who built ban evasion classifiers for Wikipedia wrote that moderators "cannot penalize someone purely based on suspicion of ban evasion". Act when the links meet a threshold you set in advance, name the rule in the notice, and offer an appeal reviewed by someone who was not involved in the first decision. Appeals do change outcomes: on Reddit in the second half of 2025, 2.9 percent of the 77,380 appeals against account-level actions for ban evasion resulted in a reversal of action.
